analysis.one_liner: Taxes big oil companies' excess profits at 25% and puts the money into highways.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would impose a temporary tax, in effect for 2008 and 2009, of 25% on the 'windfall profits' of large oil companies — profits above what they averaged in 2003-2007, plus 10%. It applies to integrated oil companies and any producer or refiner of crude oil with over $1 billion in gross receipts. The money raised would go into the Highway Trust Fund, which pays for road and bridge repair.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and highway users, through the 25% windfall-profit tax on large oil companies being deposited into the Highway Trust Fund for road and bridge work; also the construction industry that performs federally funded road projects.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 25% excise tax for 2008 and 2009 on the excess profits of large oil companies — profits above their 2003-2007 average adjusted taxable income plus 10% [S2][S3].
Applies to integrated oil companies and to any crude oil producer or refiner with over $1 billion in gross receipts, capturing the industry's largest players [S2][S3].
Transfers all windfall-tax revenue into the Highway Trust Fund, earmarking the money for federal road programs rather than the general treasury [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large oil companies — integrated majors and big producers and refiners — which would pay 25% of their above-baseline profits for two years. To the extent they pass the cost on, consumers could face somewhat higher prices at the pump.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows companies to deduct the windfall tax payment from their income taxes, reducing the effective hit on their bottom line [S3].

Because oil companies could raise prices to cover the tax, some of the cost may have landed on consumers at the pump, though the tax only applies to profits above a high baseline, limiting how much is available to shift.
The tax is temporary — it only covers tax years beginning in 2008 and 2009 — so it would not address the Highway Trust Fund's long-term financing gap.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have redirected a slice of the oil industry's 2008-era record profits to road repair, a direct public benefit at a time of high gas prices. Its design has soft spots: the tax is deductible, and a two-year tax is a one-time clawback rather than a fix for chronic highway funding shortfalls. On balance, the benefits to drivers and highway programs outweigh a modest, temporary cost concentrated on highly profitable companies.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the bill on March 13, 2008, during a period of record oil prices [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil companies kept their 2008-2009 excess profits untaxed, and no windfall revenue went to the Highway Trust Fund. Highway programs gained nothing, but oil companies were the direct beneficiaries of inaction.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the windfall profits tax bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Windfall-profits taxes on oil companies were a major lobbying target in 2008; the industry publicly opposed such proposals.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held on the bill, so no party breakdown exists; the bill drew a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would have taxed 25% of these companies' profits above their 2003-2007 baseline for 2008 and 2009, directly clawing back record windfall earnings. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against the public benefit of funding highways from those profits.

All revenue from the tax would have flowed into the Highway Trust Fund, increasing federal money available for road and bridge projects that these firms perform. The bill's failure left that funding on the table.

They stood to benefit from better-funded roads, but could have borne part of the tax through higher pump prices if companies passed it on. Because the tax applied only to profits above a high baseline, the pass-through risk was limited.
